{{Short description|Mathematical transformation used in polymer physics}}
The '''Hubbard–Stratonovich''' ('''HS''') '''transformation''' is an exact [[mathematics|mathematical]] [[Transformation (geometry)|transformation]] invented by Russian physicist [[Ruslan L. Stratonovich]] and popularized by British physicist [[John Hubbard (physicist)|John Hubbard]]. It is used to convert a [[Particle physics|particle theory]] into its respective [[Scalar field theory|field theory]] by linearizing the [[Density matrix|density operator]] in the many-body interaction term of the [[William Rowan Hamilton|Hamiltonian]] and introducing an [[auxiliary field|auxiliary scalar field]], <math display="inline">\ \phi ~.</math> It is defined via the integral identity<ref>
  {{cite journal
    |last = Стратонович  |first = Р.Л.  |author-link = Ruslan L. Stratonovich
    |year = 1957
    |script-title=ru:Об одном методе вычисления квантовых функций распределения
    |trans-title = On a method of calculating quantum distribution functions
    |journal = Доклады АН СССР  [Proceedings of the USSR Academy of Sciences] 
    |volume = 115  |issue = 6  |pages = 1097–1100
    |lang = ru
  }}
: Translation available:
  {{cite journal
    |last = Stratonovich  |first = R.L. |author-link = Ruslan L. Stratonovich
    |year = 1958
    |title = On a method of calculating quantum distribution functions
    |journal = [[Soviet Physics Doklady]]
    |volume = 2  |page = 416
    |bibcode = 1957SPhD....2..416S
    |lang = en
  }}
</ref><ref>
  {{cite journal
    |last = Hubbard  |first = J.
    |year = 1959
    |title = Calculation of partition functions
    |journal = [[Physical Review Letters]]
    |volume = 3  |issue = 2  |pages = 77–78
    |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.3.77
    |bibcode=1959PhRvL...3...77H
  }}
</ref>

:<math display="block">
\exp\!\left(\;\! -\frac{ a }{\;\! 2 \;\!}\ x^2 \;\!\right) ~=~
\sqrt{ \frac{ 1 }{\ 2\;\!\pi\;\! a\ } \;} \; \int_{-\infty}^\infty \operatorname{d}\! \phi \;
\exp\!\left(\;\! -\frac{\ \phi^2}{\ 2\;\! a\ }\ -\ i\;\! x\;\!\phi \;\!\right)\ ,
</math>

where the real constant <math>\ a > 0 ~.</math> For matrix-valued operators, such as on-site electronic density operators<ref>
{{cite book
 |last1=Altland |first1=Simons
 |year=2010
 |title=Condensed Matter Field Theory
 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
 |isbn=9780511789984  |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511789984
}}
</ref>

:<math display="block">
\exp\!\bigl(\;\! -\rho_j\ V_{jk}\ \rho_k \;\!\bigr) ~=~
\int ~ \operatorname{D}[\phi] \; \exp\!\left(\;\! -\tfrac{\;\! 1 \;\!}{ 4 }\;\!\phi_j\ V_{jk}^{-1}\ \phi_k - i\;\!\phi_j \rho_j \;\!\right) ~.
</math>

The basic idea of the HS transformation is to reformulate a system of particles interacting through two-body potentials into a system of independent particles interacting with a fluctuating field. The procedure is widely used in [[polymer physics]], classical particle physics, [[Spin glass|spin glass theory]], electronic structure theory and discrete modelization of nuclear physics such as nuclear lattice effective field theory (NLEFT).

==Calculation of resulting field theories==
The resulting field theories are well-suited for the application of effective approximation techniques, like the [[mean field approximation]]. A major difficulty arising in the simulation with such field theories is their highly oscillatory nature in case of strong interactions, which leads to the well-known [[numerical sign problem]]. The problem originates from the repulsive part of the interaction potential, which implicates the introduction of the complex factor via the '''HS''' transformation.
